claims.text: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability at high temperature primarily because of short-range ordering.
Decreased atomic mobility caused by short-range ordering inhibits phase segregation.
The proposed initial nanoparticles contain five or more metal elements.
The proposed initial nanoparticles include low levels of noble metals.
Controlled synthesis can ensure a uniform room-temperature elemental distribution in the initial nanoparticles.
Adding 1–2 at% of a suitably chosen larger-size solute is expected to disrupt short-range ordering.
Short-range ordering reduces local diffusion paths.
The local atomic environments created by short-range order reduce interdiffusion and hinder elemental segregation.
A dopant that disrupts short-range ordering will cause phase segregation to begin earlier than in undoped nanoparticles under identical heat treatment.
A dopant that disrupts short-range ordering will produce greater chemical inhomogeneity than in undoped nanoparticles under identical heat treatment.
Undoped near-equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit slower grain coarsening than the doped nanoparticles during comparable thermal treatment.
Undoped near-equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit less compositional variation than the doped nanoparticles during comparable thermal treatment.
The proposed stabilization mechanism applies when the constituent elements are sufficiently miscible to form a solid solution.
At compositions far from equiatomic, thermodynamic driving forces for phase separation may overcome stabilization due to short-range ordering.
Strong elemental immiscibility may overcome stabilization due to short-range ordering.
No direct prior data are available on how partial disruption of short-range ordering affects long-term nanoparticle stability above 1000 K.
